newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: US urges World Court to reject Iran oil-rigs case.
newsitem.headline: US urges World Court to reject Iran oil-rigs case.

text.p: The United States urged the International Court of Justice on Monday to reject Iran's compensation request for three offshore oil platforms destroyed by U.S. warships almost 10 years ago.
The disputed events date back to the final stages of the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war when the U.S. sent naval forces to the Gulf to protect international shipping.
Iran has asked the U.N. court to rule that attacks on the oil platforms in October 1987 and April 1988 violated international law and that the U.S. should pay damages.
But Washington says the strikes were a legitimate military response to attacks on a U.S. frigate and a Kuwaiti tanker sailing under the U.S. flag.
In his opening statement U.S. State Department lawyer Michael Matheson said Washington had acted in lawful self-defence and had not intervened to help Iraq's war effort.
"The Iranian platforms in question were destroyed because of their use to facilitate Iranian attacks on neutral shipping, including U.S. warships and merchant vessels," he said.
U.S. navy commander Ronald Neubauer said the platforms targeted by the U.S. were being used as military facilities and were manned by military personnel.

"In addition to identifying, tracking, monitoring and targeting innocent ships for attack, these platforms served as staging and supply bases for the Iranian helicopters and small boats used in such attacks," he told the court.
The U.S. is challenging the grounds on which Iran has brought the case before the U.N. court, which must first rule on whether both states have consented to its jurisdiction.
Iran argues that this condition is satisfied by the 1955 Treaty of Amity between the two countries which says that disputes relating to the treaty are to be referred to the court.
But the U.S. says the treaty governs commercial and consular affairs and that military matters fall outside its scope.
Matheson said Iran was seeking to use the Treaty of Amity as an "expedient jurisdictional vehicle".
"We will show that the treaty has no reasonable application to the events that are at issue in this case," he said.
"Iran's application should accordingly be dismissed for want of jurisdiction," he added.
Iran is due to explain its side of the case on Thursday, with preliminary hearings on the issue of jurisdiction expected to be concluded early next week.
The head of the Iranian delegation, Zahedin Labbaf, said he was confident that the court would accept the Treaty of Amity as a valid basis for dealing with the case.

The United States has been waging an international campaign to isolate Tehran for its alleged involvement in terrorist acts against the West. Iran strongly denies such charges and says Washington is bent on toppling its Islamic government.
In August U.S. President Bill Clinton adopted a law which penalises companies investing more than $40 million a year in the oil and gas industries of Iran and Libya.

Tehran filed a suit at the Iran-U.S. Claims Tribunal in The Hague against the law and European countries also criticised the unilateral U.S. move, saying it would unfairly penalise their oil companies.
Despite the often hostile state of their bilateral relations, Tehran and Washington showed in February that they can settle disputes without outside arbitration or adjudication.

Iran dropped a case at the International Court of Justice over the shooting down in July 1988 of an Iran Air airliner by a U.S. warship after Washington agreed to compensate the families of the 248 Iranians on board who were killed.
